### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“No one errs willingly.”

Ancient Greek

“οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν ἁμαρτάνει.”

“No one errs willingly.” Also stated near the end of the Gorgias (509e), which matters because the Protagoras passage is where the argument is built, not where it is first asserted.

### Attribution notes

One of the two claims usually labelled the Socratic paradoxes — the other being that virtue is knowledge. Read on its own it sounds like a denial of responsibility; in context it follows from the premise that everyone acts toward what they believe good, so acting badly is a failure of belief rather than of will.

#### About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

### How to read this passage

Moral philosophy asks whether morality is objective, how reasons bind us, and how character, rules, and consequences relate. Traditions differ on whether duty, virtue, or outcomes come first. This passage enters that discussion through morality, knowledge.
